title: Rhythm, Meter, Tempo, and Beat in Human Music: A Cross‐Cultural Framework and Provisional Evolutionary Timeline
content:
This multidisciplinary overview clarifies the terminology, methodology, and typology of musical timing across numerous historical and ethnic music cultures, with emphasis on Western music theory. It identifies three near-universal aspects of temporal expression, several overlooked types of beat and their semantic and pragmatic characteristics, and re-assesses the concepts of “metrical” and “ametrical” within the genre framework. All identified structures of timing are plotted on a timeline of their plausible evolution.


ABSTRACT

Human music is distinguished from language and animal calls by its sophisticated temporal organization, in which rhythm plays the key role. Yet studying rhythm is complicated by a lack of clarity about how it relates to the other means of temporal organization: meter, tempo, beat, tactus, foot, pulse, divisions. This paper reviews data from music theory, history, ethnomusicology (including little-known sources), psychoacoustics, versification, historical linguistics, prosody, orchesography, organology, archeology, and anthropology to clarify the terminology for cross-cultural study of musical timing. Rhythm, meter, and tempo are identified as distinct, nearly universal aspects of musical expression, interconnected by their mutual dependence on beat. Musical traditions employ different types of beat: unitary, binary, foot-based, syllable-based, breath-based, instrumental-technique-based, body-motion-based, and formula-based, where a recurring melodic figure supplies a period without a pulse. Each generates its own typology of meter and tempo through ongoing genre application within a community of music-users. Tracking historical changes in important genres through their structural and semantic functionality makes it possible to identify and plot metrical and tempo typologies on a timeline in relation to landmark prehistoric and historic events. The timeline proposed here is a probing step toward reconstructing the general evolution of rhythm.
